doc.title: John Lamb interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clearwater Beach, Florida, March 16, 2001

title: Leaving the service and heading to Boston with $27
summary: After discharge a brief packing-house job in Vero Beach fails, and he takes a bus to Boston with $27; a porter in New York predicts he'll be back.

story.theme_name: Coming to New York: clubs, jams, and making it
story.community_name: Making it in New York: arrival, clubs and the scene

blocks.x: and all that and Oscar, those were the two major pianists at the time. He says, “yeah, I’ve heard of Ray Brown.” And he says, “there’s a guy down in Miami can do everything Ray can do.” I says, “who is that?” He says, “Sam Jones.” I didn’t know who Sam Jones was. I’d never heard of him. And later on he was working with Cannonball and quite a few others. And I met him later on in my career, yeah. Anyway I get out of the military and decide that I’d try to go back to Vero Beach. I went to Vero Beach and got a job at a packing house, you know, to make some money. And there wasn’t anything going on there. I mean everything was domestic, I tried cleaning and I wondered if I could work in a hospital as an orderly or something. And it didn’t turn out too well. I think I stayed in the packing house a little over a week or two weeks, and I had $27 saved up. I didn’t even get along with my parents, my mother at that time, because I had changed. You know when you’re in your early twenties it’s very difficult to get along with parents at that age, because I knew quite a bit. She says, “well what you should do, John,” she says, “is take this job until you can find something else.” But there was nothing else better in Vero Beach. Have you been to Vero Beach?
Well it’s a lot different today.

But it had about 16,000 people at the time. And it was a very small town. So I decided to take my $27, I said, “well I’m going to Boston to Schillinger House.” I didn’t have any money or anything like that. So I said, “I’m heading for Schillinger House.” So I hopped on the bus—

Yeah, I hopped on the bus, moved on up, and I think it was two or three days to New York. When we got there for a break the porter outside says, “where are you going?” I says, “I’m going to Boston.” He says, “what do you do?” “I’m a musician.” He said, “what are you going up there for? Everything is right here.” He says, “you’ll be back.”

Yeah. We’re taking a little break there, yeah. Yeah, “you’ll be back.” I said, “okay,” so I hopped on and went to Boston. Because I knew I had met somebody that was originally from Vero Beach by the name of Henderson and he says, “well come on up we’ll help you out.” So I went up there and I found out he was a Pullman porter. So they put me up in the Pullman porter’s place for, what, seven dollars a week. So he gave me a room and I tried to wait tables. I remember the first job I ever tried to do up there and the guy says, “you’ve got to have a tux.” I had a black suit, double breasted. It looked good, a nice, black suit.
